OPEN
This is open, and cannot be resolved with a finite computation.
Is it true that for every $1\leq k\leq n$ the largest prime divisor of $\binom{n}{k}$, say $P(\binom{n}{k})$, satisfies\[P\left(\binom{n}{k}\right)\geq \min(n-k+1, k^{1+c})\]for some constant $c>0$?
#683: [Er76d][Er79d]
number theory | 
primes | 
binomial coefficients
A theorem of Sylvester and Schur (see [Er34]) states that $P(\binom{n}{k})>k$ if $k\leq n/2$. Erdős [Er55d] proved that there exists some $c>0$ such that, whenever $k\leq n/2$,\[P\left(\binom{n}{k}\right)\gg k\log k.\]Erdős [Er79d] writes it 'seems certain' that this holds for every $c>0$, with only a finite number of exceptions (depending on $c$). Standard heuristics on prime gaps suggest that the largest prime divisor of $\binom{n}{k}$ is, for $k\leq n/2$, in fact\[>e^{c\sqrt{k}}\]for some constant $c>0$. 
This is essentially equivalent to [961].
Additional thanks to: Alfaiz and Terence Tao

 It seems easy to construct a counterexample to the main problem.
Take $n=2^t$ and $k=n-1$ $(t\geq2)$. Then $\binom{n}{k}=\binom{2^t}{1}=2^t$, so $P\!\left(\binom{n}{k}\right)=2$.
Moreover $\min(n-k+1,\;k^{1+c})=\min(2,(2^t-1)^{1+c})=2$.
Hence $P\!\left(\binom{n}{k}\right)=2\not>2$,
so $(n,k)=(2^t,2^t-1)$ is a counterexample for every $c>0$.
It seems as an infinite series of counterexamples to the main problem? Or I've missed/misunderstood something.

 As Tao points out, this is just a typo - really the annoying $n-k+1$ term is just to handle $n/2<k\leq n$ in a non-trivial way. One should really view these problems as restricted to $k\leq n/2$.
As mentioned, this is just the same as [961] (which is stated without binomial coefficients). Including both was an oversight on my part, but it feels like it would mess up too much to remove this one now.
